Converting music recordings to note-onsets and corresponding pitches is known as automatic keyboard transcription, with recent advances relying heavily on deep neural networks. In contrast, neural methods have been outperformed by traditional non-negative matrix factorization applications due to NMF's simple and interpretable framework, albeit with NMF's lack of parameter learning limiting its performance in complex tasks. This research proposes a semi-supervised convolutive NMF approach that incorporates temporal dependencies and basic knowledge from music theory to enhance model interpretation and robustness. We replace the standard multiplicative update rule with a gradient-based update rule that leverages additional information. Replacing the Gaussian noise model with a heavy-tailed Student-t distribution improves robustness against unexpected variations in music recordings. Also, by substituting a static basis matrix with a neural factorization machine that integrates explicit encodings and inputs and using a covariance precision matrix that learns from data and music theory, the model's performance is improved. Experiments on the MAPS dataset demonstrate the model's superiority over other NMF variants and competitiveness with state-of-the-art methods in automatic keyboard transcription.

A new, comprehensive approach has been developed to study the effects of relativity and rotation on the structure of real stars. This approach can be adapted for use with any equation of state, including non-relativistic ones. The method's effectiveness has been demonstrated through the creation of rotating sequences for both relativistic and non-relativistic stars, using neutron stars and the ideal gas as models. Furthermore, this approach has successfully reproduced observed stellar properties, such as the mass asymmetry seen in GW190412 and the 1.4 solar mass limit in pulsar measurements.

A major hurdle in creating models that can automatically process and analyze complex documents is obtaining a large collection of images paired with accurate labels. To tackle this problem, we propose a method that uses a model to predict labels for a large number of unlabeled documents, then focuses on reviewing only the ones it's least confident about. This approach, which we call bi-directional labeling, was tested on two types of challenging documents: legal decisions and scientific abstracts. It proved to be significantly more efficient than other methods, requiring about one-tenth of the number of paired images to achieve a certain level of accuracy. It also resulted in a substantial reduction in the cost of producing these models, with our method requiring only about one-eighth of the resources compared to other approaches.

Researchers have investigated using deep learning techniques to quickly and effectively classify neutron star-black hole merger signals, also known as gravitational waves.  A deep learning model called Deep Learning Signal Generation and Classification was created and its performance was evaluated against other classification techniques.  The study found that the model could accurately identify the type of merger at a rate of 99% within just 0.1 seconds, outperforming other methods in both processing time and classification accuracy.  To further validate the model's effectiveness, the researchers applied it to real gravitational wave data and were able to correctly classify a merger event at a rate of 95%.  A notable achievement of this research was the first time the model was able to accurately classify a neutron star-destroying merger event, demonstrating its potential to provide rapid and reliable results within the designated coincidence window.  Overall, the study highlights the efficiency of deep learning methods for processing gravitational wave data and contributing to the overall detection rate of these events.  A corresponding code is available online at https://github.com/yjy2017/DLSGC.

This paper introduces the Marker-driven Neural Network (MarkNet) framework, a framework that allows the use of domain knowledge to define the structure of a neural network. MarkNet consists of two key components: a meta-network that identifies useful features or "markers" from data, and a target network that uses these markers to make predictions. We utilized the MarkNet framework to address the social wellness prediction challenge, where we aim to identify social wellness scores from online discussions and user profiles in virtual communities. As neural metaparametric models are currently under-researched, our work represents one of the early applications of this framework to a real-world problem. Converting the social wellness estimation problem into a set of related Bayesian estimations of social features, our neural metaparametric model successfully predicts social wellness scores by leveraging these estimates. Experimental results show significant improvements in social wellness prediction accuracy compared to baseline models.

This paper builds upon the work of  Davis,  Goldman,  Morse  and  Steele  who studied a scallop that can change its shape and moves through a viscous environment by alternately closing and opening its shell. Using an established model from their study, we analyze the optimal movement of this two-state scallop with varying mouth sizes and body shapes that can be adjusted during its closed state. Through multiple distinct scenarios, we demonstrate the robustness of a key result from their paper and provide insights into the stability of the optimal movement, supply and demand curves, and how the choice of mouth size affects the efficiency of the scallop's movement.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, the rapid changes in social behavior significantly impacted the spread of the virus and urban poverty levels. However, existing models of how people move through cities and the economic consequences of these models failed to account for sudden shifts in human behavior. Furthermore, most approaches treated human movement as uniform across different social groups, ignoring the varying dynamics that influenced the pandemic's trajectory and urban inequality. This study introduces a sophisticated framework for understanding urban poverty lanes based on varying social behavior, utilizing data from location services in over 800 cities across 38 countries. Findings reveal that the pandemic amplified urban inequality in some regions while having little effect in others, with the location of poverty lanes shifting in response to peak infection rates in a peak-driven, asymmetric manner. This study suggests that the sudden, asymmetric nature of social behavior is a crucial aspect of how people move through cities, which should be incorporated into the design and evaluation of public health policies and the development of urban-focused machine learning models.

The formation process of a massive star is thought to be intermittent and linked to its significant mass accumulation through mergers with other small-sized stars. To test this hypothesis, a new method using submillimeter observations and optical data has been implemented to study early-stage massive star formation. By focusing on ten young stellar objects, researchers detected massive, dynamically significant mergers for five of them, with at least one probable merger event contributing to the overall dynamics. The proposed method is versatile and can be applied to other merging systems to gain deeper insights into the intricate relationship between massive star formation and its probable merger events.

For a class of type III factors, we prove a correspondence between two different constructions of wedge-local observables: one using endomorphisms performed by Longo and Witten, and another using a specific construction by Fermi fields. This proof provides a connection between quantum field theory and Cuntz algebras. Additionally, we plan to apply this result to demonstrate the unitary equivalence of the Chiral Fermi Field and the Scattering Matrix endomorphisms, which were previously shown to be unitarily equivalent by Longo and Witten.

The controversy surrounding 5G technology's safety has sparked our interest in exploring the radiation it emits near sensitive locations such as educational facilities and medical centers. Unlike previous studies, we have created a more accurate model by using real building data and a advanced 3D simulation to determine how much 5G radiation is emitted over children, teenagers, students, and patients. By analyzing various scenarios and accounting for real-world variability, we were able to provide a comprehensive overview of the radiation levels, which, despite being within international safety guidelines,显示出 potentially significant differences from earlier research.

This research develops a Hamiltonian Dysthe equation for deep-water gravity waves, whose surface area is relatively large, in scenarios where the initial flow's vorticity remains consistent, characterized by the curl being constant.

We propose a novel framework for differential calculus on convex spaces, focusing on locally convex 'terrains'. Our proposal builds upon earlier work by differential analysts by simplifying the underlying mathematical structures, specifically by working with locally convex functions defined on convex sets and determining their associated differential fields. Our framework enables the expression of integral formulas, with the local version of the divergence theorem being demonstrated through a straightforward proof. Additionally, an exemplary application is provided to illustrate how this approach can be utilized.

This research completes the exploration of sonar data sonification, with a focus on sonar sonification. Unlike previous studies, this work examines the impact of multiple overlapping sonar scans, which is typical in navigation systems. To achieve this goal, a sonar blending technique has been developed to manage and integrate sonar data from various scans, ensuring consistency in sonar sonification and enhancing system performance. A proposed sonar blending method manages the alignment and integration of multiple sonar scans while minimizing system computational load through efficient data management. A corresponding sonar sonification filter called the Modified Generalized Proportional Integral Derivative (MGPID) has been developed to ensure smooth and coherent sonar sonification in this context. The proposed system's efficacy is demonstrated via ocean trials and visualized via data sonograms and video analyses.

The amount of online information has significantly increased, which although beneficial also poses challenges in terms of efficiency. This problem is particularly apparent in the realm of news, where users spend excessive time reading various articles. To alleviate this issue, automated text summarization techniques can be employed to address multiple challenges. Although these methods were initially developed for researchers, their application can be extended to include the efficiency of ordinary users as well. The primary objective of this research is to investigate the potential of utilizing automatic summarization techniques in improving the effectiveness of FakeNews detector systems. The results of the experiments conducted on the 2016 Facebook News Dataset yielded two key findings, namely that generated summaries retain significant original information, although some distortion occurs. Additionally, the experiment demonstrated that replacing full news articles with their corresponding summaries does lead to marginally reduced performance, ultimately indicating the potential for summarization techniques to enhance the efficiency of classifiers.

This work investigates the theoretical underpinning of the "bending influence" in random field geometry, a concept that has gained popularity due to its practical applications in geostatistics and earth sciences. We provide a rigorous mathematical analysis based on Gaussian random fields, focusing on geodesic curvature. This study investigates the asymptotic behavior of geodesic curvature integrals along highly curved curves as the domain of the random field expands. Under specific technical conditions, we establish that these integrals converge to a normal distribution, and the limit varies depending on the curve's shape, with specific examples and simulations providing insights into this phenomenon.

To secure Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (NOMA) against malicious base stations, this research proposes an innovative decision-coupled code (DCC) that links the instruction decoded by the malicious base station with the data it receives. The proposed scheme employs linear codes for both decryption and detection, utilizing a novel criterion to evaluate the security of the DCC candidates. The mortality probability, representing the likelihood of a failed decryption, inference, or detection, is formulated and analyzed for the DCC. Theoretical and numerical findings demonstrate that specific DCC candidates can achieve enhanced mortality probabilities, indicative of improved security, in comparison to conventional alternatives.

Detecting anomalies and identifying key information in high-dimensional data sets is an extensively studied problem. This challenge can be effectively addressed by examining a variation of the data distribution or isolating data points with exceptional values. In this paper, we reframe the problem of inspection and Intensive investigation using a optimization problem that considers both correlation and sparsity. This reformulation distinguishes itself from other works by utilizing an equivalence between IPCE and a simplified model. We then introduce a new method to solve this problem by integrating techniques from convex optimization and high-dimensional statistical analysis. This algorithm combines iterative transformations and weighted correlations to efficiently solve the problem by utilizing the data's covariance and sparsity structures. Furthermore, we prove that the convergence of this algorithm occurs at a steady, predictable rate. This research is conducted under the assumption of Gaussian data distributions, where our approach benefits from pre-conditioning to handle cases of infinite convergence.

The growth in volume of Web 2.0 data has posed significant challenges for
Web mining tasks, particularly in defining accurate labels for online comments
and reviews by analyzing their content. While several programs exist to help
manually classify the content, they are often inefficient due to starting from
scratch and lacking the ability to incorporate pre-existing classifications or
account for emotional expressions found in reviews. This study proposes a BERT-
based method to generate initial classifications and adjust them based on the
emotional content of online comments, specifically tailored for Facebook page
comments. By utilizing a pre-trained BERT model to generate detailed semantic
annotations, the model leverages Bayesian Classification to generate initial
labels and Support Vector Regression to adjust the labels based on the emotion
expressed, demonstrating its- ability to utilize emotional expressions to
improve the accuracy of manual labeling. By forming a small adjustment model,
it is possible to significantly reduce the workload of starting from scratch when
labeling new data, while also considering the emotional expressions found in
reviews. By integrating the BERT model with emotion classifications, the model
demonstrates its- ability to generate accurate labels for online comments and
reviews, thereby helping to improve the efficiency of manual labeling tasks.

The objective of this study is to provide a theoretical framework for analyzing complex, real-world scenarios in politics and sports where competitors leverage past outcomes to predict and influence future results. This work investigates the behavior of multiple players participating in a sequence of games played on an infinite, linear scale. Each player receives a numerical outcome based on their position and uses this history of results, along with past pattern recognition, to make decisions in subsequent games. The research reveals unavoidable flaws in several widely accepted methodological approaches and exposes the limited applicability of perfect reasoning systems, specifically those aligned with S4 and T4 modal logics. Furthermore, the study confirms that practical, statistically-based methodologies can still be beneficial despite these limitations.

We analyzed a significant number of X-ray polars observed by Chandra for which we have optical spectroscopic data, noting the presence or absence of asynchronous precession in their jets. We determined the spectral parameters of each observation, including photon indices, and found that the distribution of photon indices for asynchronous polars without hard X-rays is skewed towards values lower than those of their asynchronous counterparts and normal polars. We hypothesize that the lower photon indices observed in some asynchronous polars are linked to differences in the accretion processes, possibly related to the alignment of the magnetic field and the accretion disk.

This paper presents an innovative approach to resolving fluid-structure interaction problems by linking and dividing the Reduced Basis Method (RBM) into two distinct parts. Initially, we will explore the implementation of a reduced model for the fluid and structural components using coupled RBM. Subsequently, we will examine the utilization of a reduced model comprising separate RBMs for both the fluid and structure, ensuring the balance of forces and velocities at the interface through the partitioned RBM technique. The method's effectiveness will be demonstrated through the simulation of flag fluctuation issues induced by periodic fluid flow.

In autonomous navigation, creating efficient map representations is crucial for non-holonomic vehicles to successfully and quickly find their way through complex environments. Current research focuses on grid-based maps, utilizing algorithms like SLAM to generate them. While effective, these methods can be resource-intensive and slow when processing large environments. For navigation, a map needs to capture the overall spatial layout, allowing for efficient path planning and localization. Recent approaches using graph neural networks and topological methods have shown promise, but often struggle with real-world applications and localization. In this paper, we introduce HiTMap, a novel hierarchical framework that combines grid and topological elements for robust navigation. This approach utilizes grid maps for localization and enhances them with a graph-based layout representation, enabling efficient path finding and accurate localization through graph neural networks. Our results show significant improvements in performance, accuracy, and real-time processing when tested on real-world data.

This document describes the submission of the University of Michigan and Indiana University to the 6th SemEval-2019 Text-off Challenge, which focused on detecting aggressive language in social media posts. Two distinct models were developed for this challenge, including a BERT-based approach and an SVM-based method using preprocessed lexicons.

This research focuses on enhancing atomic interferometry with a Meissner effect to simultaneously take advantage of the high precision of atomic time with which to measure changes in a local magnetic field and the strong Meissner effect with which to detect changes in a local electric field. A test mass with atoms inside experiences a pronounced Meissner effect in response to even small local electric field alterations, while the atoms' acceleration is significantly amplified by that same effect. Both atomic interference patterns can be harnessed to measure these parameters, where the precise timing provided by atomic time delivers a significant advantage to sensibility, specifically with which to detect very small local electric field changes and very small local magnetic field changes with exceptional accuracy and sensitivity. This approach allows for sensitive measurements of local electric field alterations and local magnetic field changes with atomic interferometry by leveraging the Meissner effect, specifically with which to achieve extraordinary accuracy and sensitivity.

The distinctive properties of two-dimensional materials can be significantly altered by reducing them to single layers, enabling the emergence of novel phenomena like magnetocaloric effects (MCE) in certain two-dimensional systems. In this study, we investigate the interplay between spin-orbit coupling and closeness-induced exchange in two-dimensional metal dichalcogenides using a tight-binding model, incorporating both types of couplings in a non-equivalent honeycomb structure. The examination involves analyzing the system's density of states, self-consistent Fermi levels, and magnetic and caloric properties through Landau Fermi-liquid theory. Our findings indicate that a critical threshold of closeness-induced exchange can trigger the spontaneous polarization of the spin-polarized sub-systems near the critical point, accompanied by a significant enhancement in the magnetic entropy change at this point. The examination of the non-equivalent honeycomb structure reveals an asymmetry in the magnetic entropy change with respect to the applied field direction, which can be effectively amplified by adjusting the parameters of the two types of spin-orbit coupling.

The behavior of gap-plasmons in bifilular conductive systems is examined across different gaps, specifically focusing on how the electron spill-over and nonlocal effects influence their dispersion as the gap decreases. Both a rigorous boundary condition and an approximate nonlocal model were utilized to represent these influences. Findings from both approaches show convergence and reveal a key distinction: at small gaps, the spill-over/nonlocal model yields the correct energy density behavior, whereas a local model with distinct boundaries produces unrealistic results. Furthermore, the findings indicate that gap-plasmon dispersion can be effectively understood through a dual perspective, combining local dynamics within the gaps and the flow of spillover electrons fueling adjacent conductive layers, effectively bridging large and small gap regimes.

A robust normalization process is proposed to mitigate the impact of malformed terms, potentially caused by hacking attempts or data corruption. To maintain correctness, we slightly modify the Calculus of Constructions, then develop and slow-down arrow-based type checking. An example is provided linking to the code on GitHub.

To provide an intuitive understanding of topological quantum phenomena, we have created educational tools that simplify complex ideas. We focused on the solvable Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, where we can clearly illustrate the count of localized electrons at a material's end using both visual and numerical methods. We have developed two versions of these tools - an interactive graphical program written in C++, and an inline JavaScript version accessible via web browsers, allowing both in-person and remote students to participate. Additionally, we have prepared supplementary teaching resources, including answers to common questions students ask during laboratory sessions.

We have developed a geometric framework to provide an intuitive understanding of finite mixture models, revealing their connections with probability, geometry, and non-additive measures. By leveraging this framework, we can rederive key properties of mixture models, such as the likelihood being concave in geometric space, its equivalence to a expected value under a measure that obeys the Choquet rule, and its EMM to a optimal path in a curved geometric setting. Furthermore, we have obtained a distinct expression for the EMM using the geodesic structure.

Using the CFT/Dual-loop approach, we re-examine the supersymmetric gauge theory/AdS5 x S5 gravity duality for finite coupling and expand around a specific regime where the 't Hooft coupling is large but not infinitely large, or 't Hooft coupling is infinite but not exclusively so. This analysis reverts to the standard duality at certain points. We look into the characteristics of the Dual-loop approach, especially in relation to the standard duality, and compare it to the worldsheet sigma model at infinite 't Hooft coupling. This comparison highlights the standard Duality as having a more comprehensive understanding than the infinite coupling sigma model. We outline the principles of the Dual-loop approach, and using them, derive the two-loop correction to the semi-classical expansion of a generic superstring state, validating previous findings. Additionally, we derive the 3-loop correction for this state, matching earlier direct calculations.

Objects on GPGPUs are managed through concurrent memory allocation, allowing any of them to access and read global memory without synchronization, leading to a performance bottleneck due to diverse memory access patterns. While several frameworks exist to develop GPGPG applications, they often lack flexibility, requiring significant code modification to adapt to specific hardware and limiting the use of high-level object-oriented features. To overcome these limitations, a novel memory allocator called DynaSOAr has been created, which utilizes sofield structures to efficiently allocate contiguous memory blocks for related objects, thereby leveraging spatial locality and enabling the use of advanced object-oriented features, all while maintaining framework-like properties.

This paper investigates the boundedness of specific operators, including sublinear operators and commutators, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces.
The underlying operators satisfy the standard size condition and have additional restrictions, particularly on Riesz potentials.
A key lemma is established to support these investigations, followed by several boundedness criteria derived from this lemma.
The topic of boundedness for sublinear operators and mixed Morrey spaces is also explored, with some relevant results presented.
The article then examines the boundedness of the central maximal operator and the fractional integral on mixed Herz-type spaces.

Leads quantum states around nanoscale structures significantly impact their electronic and scattering properties, with d-f adatoms on cubic surfaces having unpaired electrons that contribute to magnetic moments.  These properties can be understood through a modified version of the s-d exchange Heisenberg Hamiltonian, which accounts for the difference between the d and s exchange interactions.  In this work, a first-principles approach is used to study the d-f adatoms and dimers on a planar surface, with the focus being on the formation of a hybridized singlet state resulting from the hybridization of d and s orbitals with the surface.  By comparing the results of this quantum model to those of full-density functional theory, it is found that the exchange field in the s-band is overestimated due to correlation effects that are neglected in this theory.  Furthermore, it is shown that the exchange field can be manipulated by adjusting the distance between the adatoms or by applying an external electric field to the system.  In the case of localized d-states, a weak field can be used to switch the helical spin texture of the rs-states from left to right.  However, this switch requires a stronger field for hybridized d-f adatoms, and it is also possible to switch the spin texture by adjusting the distance between the adatoms in an f-f dimer.  This work provides key insights into the design of spintronic devices that rely on resonant structures.

Our proposal, FourierMask, is an implicit functional instance segmentation network. FourierMask utilizes a FourierMapping to represent three-dimensional space, converting it into a custom implicit function. This allows FourierMask to predict the value of any coordinate with ease. In comparison to traditional networks, FourierMask achieves more accurate value predictions using fewer parameters. We have incorporated optimization techniques and a custom loss function to maximize its efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate FourierMask's superiority over competing models on both synthetic and complex real-world data sets, particularly when dealing with objects characterized by intricate surfaces.

Let $M$ be a smooth, closed, oriented manifold of dimension $2k-1$, with $k$ being an integer greater than or equal to 2. Let $m$ be an integer greater than or equal to $3$, with a specified set of prime factors. This article provides a detailed analysis of the localized invariant, known as the confined homology, for the space of oriented diffusion maps from $M$ to $m$-dimensional tori, denoted as $\mathcal{ConfMap}(M,m\text{-torus})$. Through computation of the confined homology, we establish the existence of oriented diffusion maps that cannot be homotopically deformed to a specific point, for a broad category of pairs $(M,m\text{-torus})$.

Our research employs satellite imagery from multiple angular viewpoints, provided by MISR and MODIS, to analyze complex, convective clouds that are difficult to penetrate. Using a simplified model, we modify traditional radiative transfer simulations to efficiently predict how light travels through these cloudy areas. By comparing these simulations to actual satellite observations, we are able to locate a region of extreme opacity within the clouds where light barely penetrates. Studying this "veiled core" region allows us to gain valuable insights into how clouds scatter light and regulate the amount of solar radiation that reaches Earth's surface. Our analysis focuses primarily on the lower portions of these clouds, utilizing advanced techniques to smooth out variations in cloud properties. Key parameters affecting light scattering, including the size, composition, and arrangement of ice crystals within the clouds, significantly impact our findings and should be considered when interpreting our results. Ultimately, by studying the dense core regions of these clouds from multiple angles, we can enhance our understanding of cloud physics and cooling capabilities, as well as pave the way for similar investigations of complex aerosols and young asteroids shrouded in dust.

To counteract gradual radiation that reduces a translating translucible ship's mass over time, utilizing self-generated power for propulsion is more effective than external light collection. To significantly extend the benefits of translation, reducing friction losses that diminish as a result of radiation should be considered. This reduction in friction related speed losses can be achieved through the use of ion propulsion systems powered by that collected radiation. The implementation of such systems on the translucible ship allows for net power conservation and the maintenance of constant mass, despite the gradual loss of that mass due to the radiation. Furthermore, the application of chirp message content within the transmitted radiation enables listeners to discern the encoded information despite the varying frequency and intensity that results from the radiation.

To determine the age and composition of planetary systems, astronomers employ various methods including astrophysical, spectroscopic, and geochronological approaches.  In this study, a new exoplanet was discovered, TOI-712 b, and multiple techniques were employed to analyze its characteristics.  TOI-512 is similar to nearby stars like Sun, where TOI-712 appears to be more active and cooler, providing a suitable environment for the planet's development.  TOI-712 b, along with two additional planets TOI-712 c and d, were detected and analyzed, exhibiting moderate sizes under 2.5 Earth radii, occupying the so-called "mini-Kepler gap".  Based on stellar activity, TOI-712's age is estimated at between approximately 2.7 billion to 4.5 billion years old, and its semi-major axis suggests the TOI-712 system may be in a transitional phase of development.  TOI-712 presents an unusual opportunity to study the characteristics of an evolving planetary system that could provide insights into the evolution of similar systems including our own solar system.

This paper explores the cause of magnetic properties observed in rutile TiO2 doped with certain elements using Density Functional Theory.  A key question arises whether these magnetic properties stem from a lack of electrons or unpaired electrons in the 3d Ti orbitals. A thorough analysis of C-doped TiO2 was conducted where the total electron count was kept the same as in C2N2-doped TiO2. It was found that even with an equal number of electrons, ferromagnetism could still occur due to the redistribution of electrons within the 3d Ti orbitals. Furthermore, introducing slight distortions to the unit cell could also induce ferromagnetic behavior. A possible explanation for this phenomenon is provided by examining the overlap of atomic orbitals. A simpler, user-friendly descriptor for this electron redistribution is also proposed.

This letter describes the difficulty in generating top-quark pairs at a collider detector due to the significant momentum that characterizes such events. Furthermore, we suggest an innovative method for identifying the production of top-quark pairs that do not decay into visible final states using the characteristics of charged particles that are globally connected in the event. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach with simulated data for both standard and non-standard scenarios, specifically those involving an associated production of a top-quark and an $W$ boson. We find that our method can achieve a sensitivity to signal-to-background ratios of 1:100 to 1:20 for a wide spectrum of processes, including those involving an elastic scattering of a quark and a $W$ boson.

Our investigation into the intra-cluster medium's turbulence using spectral line variations continues, specifically examining structure functions of the projected two-dimensional maps. However, current spectral measurements are significantly impacted by inaccuracies and uncertainties, especially towards the edges of the observed cluster area, which limits their reliability for analyzing turbulent fluctuations. As such, certain regions must be excluded from further consideration, which may distort the assumed turbulent structure conforming to Levy distributions. Given the insufficient observational data to fully validate or reject this hypothesis, the current study highlights the critical importance of next-generation, highly accurate and large-scale spectral line observations for a more comprehensive understanding of the intra-cluster medium's turbulent nature.

This paper builds upon a recent development by Guo, Wu, and Yang (2019), which extended the concepts of Ramsey properties and upper richness to a new property called Ramsey upper richness. We have proven that for any compact, connected graph without self-edges, there exists a upper bound on the p-th power of its edges, such that if it is colored with at least two distinct colors, a specific, connected, monochromatic, power-of-edged, isomorphic graph is guaranteed to be present. This upper bound holds true for any number of edges, p, greater than or equal to 3. Furthermore, we have established that for the family of all such, connected, graph, there is no single, upper limit on the number of colors required to satisfy this condition. We have also explored the upper bounds of this condition for specific graph types, including cycle and theta graphs.

Located at the heart of the Galactic Center, the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) contains an anomalous, Anisotropic Mass Configuration (AMC) with a distinct elongated shape. This feature can be clearly seen in near-infrared and millimeter wavelength images, however its effects are unclear in sub-millimeter images. A new method involving 2D correlation functions provides a clear visual representation of both structural and spectral characteristics, revealing significant AMC features in the CMZ at various wavelengths. The results indicate that these visible AMC patterns in the CMZ's near-infrared and millimeter images disappear in the Mapster 850$\mu$m sub-millimeter image. Nevertheless, our research indicates that small-scale AMC features in the CMZ's magnetic field may have been smoothed out as per the Mapster data. A limitation of our study includes a reduced resolution due to the need for both spatial and spectral deconvolution, resulting in a diagonal broadening effect on the correlation maps.

Eye-centered Detection (ECD) is a method to identify Bell's paralysis by identifying the eye that is closed or weakly open in a video. This study proposes three versions of eye-centered features: skin color separation, eye-shaped features, and features extracted from an SegNet network. Our experiments were conducted on self-recorded videos and those from publicly available databases. The results show that skin color features performed best with 89.13 F-scores when using a SegNet network to extract eye features. This performance improved to 75.74 F-scores with videos that natural lighting and 68.81 F-scores with lower quality videos that include variations in lighting and angles.

In the lattice formulation of QED, artificial noise from qubit interactions causes spontaneous photon creation even in vacuums. Our study utilizes a novel, three-level system, or qutrit, based superconducting circuit to suggest that adding extra energy levels can mitigate this noise. By comparing the dynamics of sQED with qubits and sQED with qutrits, we find that the lattice noise in sQED with qutrits is substantially reduced, providing a potential pathway for more stable and noise-resilient simulations.

Our analysis reveals significant enhancements in the generation of spin-polarized positrons when laser-exposed metal foil targets are subjected to intense pulsing lasers in the terawatt range. These findings are based on detailed simulations that incorporate the interaction between lasers and targets, the behavior of generated electron positron pairs, and the impact on already existing electrons. Key strategies for achieving high levels of positron polarization include utilizing targets with aligned magnetic properties and taking into consideration the orientation of the lasers. The proposed method will be highly effective in feeding polarization-retaining positron injectors for the production of spin-controlled e+e- beams through acceleration in plasma or near conventional radiators.

Finite groups can be classified by whether their communication cost grows at most polynomially with size. Recent research focused on determining which specific types of groups have constant communication cost, particularly those with limited exponential growth rate. A newly discovered infinite family of groups with constant rate of polynomial growth has been identified as having constant-cost generating sets, but contains subgroups that require an infinite number of elements to be identified. This finding was recently confirmed by both experimental simulation and rigorous mathematical proof. In addition, some groups with complex structure were shown to be completely connectable through two elements using breadth-first search, as were numerous smaller groups analyzed through a broad database.

This paper introduces an innovative temperature detector designed for precise low-voltage applications.  The proposed detector is capable of converting static temperature readings into digital data and features an innovative temperature-sensing mechanism.  It utilizes a straightforward, supply-voltage-independent method to convert temperature differences into proportional chip currents.  The method employs a 10-bit current-stepped analog-to-digital converter (ASIC) to determine the temperature.  With a 0.6V$-$1.8V supply, the system consumes 2.6nW and 14.4$\mu$J per conversion at 0.7C and 1.5V, respectively.  The ASIC can detect temperatures as low as 0.24{\deg}C with a conversion time of 1$\mu$s.  It operates effectively across a wide temperature range from $-40^\circ$C to $85^\circ$C, with an area of 0.0178mm$^2$.  The system demonstrates reliable performance across 50 randomly selected chips.

The general stability of magnetised stars with axial symmetry needs further study. 
Here, the basic structure of these stars will be assumed to be the same as that of a star with magnetic fields aligned on the axis. 
Using the method developed by Balachandran and Benjamin, the equations of stellar dynamics will be adapted to this axial symmetry and the effects of magnetic fields will be incorporated using the method established by Chandrasekhar and Kadantseff. 
The resulting equation will then be analysed using the method established by Balachandran and Beniamin for specific models to determine stability conditions. 
It has been discovered in this study that axial symmetry in magnetic fields influences both the overall stability of the star and the specific conditions required for stability. 
Notably, this condition is dependent on the orientation of the magnetic fields. 
If the magnetic fields are directed axially, the effect of the magnetic fields on stability is always favourable, but in cases where the magnetic fields are not aligned with the axis, the effect could be both beneficial and detrimental to stability.

In this study, we deliver a precise numerical solution for the flow equations of the relativistic quantum field theory, a topic that follows from the broader understanding of the non-equilibrium dynamics in relativistic quantum systems. Our solution method leverages the relationship between FRRG and LFT, where we transform the full quantum flow into a set of finite, non-equilibrium fluid dynamics equations and solve them using computational methods. We apply this approach to flow equations for FRG effective actions in relative functional renormalization-group theory and local functional renormalization-group theory and establish a connection to non-equilibrium density functional theory. We utilize a simplified model, the $O(N)$ $\phi^4$ theory, to demonstrate that initial state preparations described by an effective action flow towards a theory in the absolute equilibrium state as per the Hohenberg-Mermin-Wagner theorem. We analyze the impact of initial preparation on the final state density matrix's diagonal elements. We examine the convergence of the time-Expansion of the density matrix based on its associated coefficients derived from the effective action. We investigate the convergence rates for flows originating from different initial states, particularly those derived from an $S$-matrix, a fully factorized effective action, and a partially factorized effective action. We observe distinct convergence patterns and rates, including the influence of the number of fields in interaction terms and the presence of time-dependent interaction terms that cause mixing in the density matrix. We further explore whether a final state can be achieved within

Music information retrieval techniques depend heavily on high-quality annotated data, but obtaining annotated tracks at scale is both costly and labor-intensive. Recent advancements in audio-to-text technology have produced large datasets containing initial text labels for entire music collections. To examine the effectiveness of these preliminary labels, we encourage community input via the Pied Piper platform, a web-based system that pairs each track with its corresponding label and enables users to provide feedback on a substantial stride. Based on the gathered annotations from this system, we assess the quality of the pre-labels and integrate them into enhanced datasets. Furthermore, we leverage the gathered annotations to enhance retrieval performance on the evaluated datasets and the PIER platform.

This work delves into various geometric structures within Lie groupoids and smooth stacks, including connections, curvature, connections bundle, principal bundles, associated bundles, characteristic classes, and connections on Lie algebroids. A unifying approach is presented through a Lie pseudo-group, a specific class of Lorentzian groups and Lie groupoids. Notably, a smooth stack version of a recent theorem is also examined, which ensures the equivalence of two structures when their underlying Lie algebroids are equivalent, involving torsion, curvature, and connection data.

A dark molecular ridge in the Draco infant star-forming region appears as a series of core structures, potentially indicating an advanced development stage. Observations from the SubMillimeter Array and Planck space telescope revealed a total length of 16 parsecs for this ridge, which is not random. The ridge is composed of multiple concentric shells connected by longitudinal filaments, which is a fundamental feature of star formation models. The ridge is also not isolated, as it is connected to surrounding gas and the halo observed in the region. A proposed name for this distinctive morphology is a "dark island." The development of the Draco core consists of three primary stages: initial gas collapse leading to the formation of a central dense core, subsequent core expansion due to gravitational instability resulting in the formation of a dense ridge, and final core and ridge maturation leading to the formation of massive protostars within dense regions.

Godel modal logics can be viewed as extensions of basic propositional Godel logics by a necessity operator, and this study delves into the underlying algebraic and relational frameworks for certain types of Godel logics, and some of their extensions. The algebraic and relational frameworks for a range of these logics, including some that incorporate tolerance and transitivity principles, are examined and characterized in detail. Additionally, the algebraic and relational frameworks for the corresponding Matnetics systems are investigated.

LiDAR point clouds obtained from multi-sensor systems yield rich information that can be leveraged in training artificial intelligence models. These models are capable of inferring high-level information from the data, including object identification and behavior prediction. However, utilizing LiDAR point clouds for training presents several challenges due to the discrepancy between the abundant raw data and the relatively small datasets with corresponding target labels. To mitigate this challenge, researchers have developed specialized LiDAR datasets with comprehensive labels, although they often fall short in capturing diverse scenarios and extensive annotations necessary for validating the robustness of machine learning models. This work seeks to contribute novel LiDAR data with detailed labels that can facilitate object detection, behavior analysis, and model refinement by potentially transferring learning models from well-annotated datasets to real-world applications with minimal labeled data.

The study of correlations between random quantities is a key aspect of probability theory and statistics, with numerous applications, including analyzing the behavior of random quantities as they progress over time, space, or complexity. This work develops a general technique for calculating expected products of the form E[Ψ_a(ξ_1,...,ξ_k)Ψ_b(ξ_1,...,ξ_k)] where random quantities are defined by an existing system and two distinct functions, leading to a versatile framework for analyzing the calculated products as the underlying parameters change. This new method is then used to establish new results and strengthen known calculations of quantitative properties for random quantities formed from the unit sphere, a binary random matrix, and the Riemann zeta function.

The Pierre Auger Observatory in Argentina has been utilized to study the correlation of Ultra-High Energy Cosmic Rays (UHECRs) and high-energy neutrinos from IceCube, utilizing the directional distribution of UHECRs and the energy spectrum of neutrinos to derive a neutrino-UHECR coincidence rate. The 13-year IceCube data and the Auger 1.5-degree and 3-degree binned spectra have also been employed to calculate the coincidence rate, with the latter incorporating more accurate uncertainties. The more uncertain backward-binned neutrino data have also been included in the coincidence rate calculation. Furthermore, an innovative graphical tool called the Concordance Curve has been created to visually represent the coincidence rate as a function of both neutrino and UHECR energies. The coincidence rate with the most probable UVFit parameters and the 1-sigma uncertainty range has been calculated, as have the ratio of the coincidence rate to the product of the neutrino and UHECR fluxes and the required dark matter properties to explain the observed phenomena if the Universe consists solely of dark matter. The required dark matter properties would fall within the acceptable range for stable dark matter within a specific probability range, as constrained by other observations. The Concordance Curve's ability to visually represent the coincidence rate can also be utilized for other research purposes, such as examining the relationship between solar flares and VERA detected neutrinos or radio bursts and VERA detected neutrinos.

The behavior of liquid foams remains an unresolved challenge in the study of complex fluids.  We investigate the properties of liquid foams under shear stress, focusing on a specific friction-like relation that seems to apply universally.  By analyzing a wide range of foams, we find that their interfacial tension directly influences their viscous response to shear, similar to the Mohr-Coulomb law found in other disciplines.  Our study reveals the origin of this relationship and provides a theoretical explanation based on the foams' elastic properties and statistical pressure transmission patterns.  As a result, we can predict the foam's viscous response based on its texture and make measurements to validate our theory's underlying assumptions.  Ultimately, this finds that the foam's interfacial tension is a critical parameter that defines its viscous response to shear stress, affecting the viscosity's variation with density in both dry and gyrotropic foams.

This report focuses on classifying images of various skin cancers including benign and malignant tumors using deep learning and entropy techniques. We employed transfer learning with the Inception v3 network and combined it with either sigmoid or softmax output layers. An additional entropy-based stage was used to incorporate disk entropy and binary cross-entropy into an SVM for enhanced classification. We tested two configurations with distinct entropy approaches and found both outperformed a single classifier, with an outperformance of at least 0.1 in accuracy over baseline methods on two different datasets. To handle imbalance in classification, we applied weighted SVM with equalization of class counts. Furthermore, we investigated using only the Inception in an alternative setup and found it yielded lower accuracy than at best 0.9 in comparing multiple classifiers. However, incorporating the entropy stage to manage outlier samples improved performance, with accuracy rising from 0.85 to 0.94 after incorporating both entropies.

We are investigating a complex phenomenon that occurs when a viscous fluid, spinning within a Hele-Shaw cell, tries to displace another fluid that is centered and stationary. This phenomenon features an asymmetry due to the spinning motion and often displays fingerlike structures. In order to understand the fingerprint-like patterns, we developed a model that can describe the system's behavior globally. Our approach yielded an effective equation of state and led to the discovery of two distinct types of fingers that can coexist. We observed that the number of these fingers is controlled by a parameter that arises from the asymptotic behavior of the system. Furthermore, we found that the fingerlike structure is most pronounced when this parameter has a specific value, and we developed a way to estimate the value of this parameter based on the system's asymptotic behavior.

Time-reversal symmetry in Hamiltonian systems typically leads to system-state confusion, undermining the applicability of statistical mechanics to certain scenarios, including the observed irreversible processes in most real-world systems. While the typical resolution involves the assumption of system-state uniqueness within a certain time and then generalizing this resolution, an excessively high standard that fails to apply to systems with large phase space variations, and is overly restrictive. Therefore, the primary focus of current approaches and theories centers on containing the phase space variations and calculating the associated matrix or probability distributions within limited ranges, which are then utilized to revise the microcanonical ensemble to cover a broad spectrum of real-world systems and processes. In contrast, the solution presented and analyzed in this paper aims to overcome the system-state confusion in Hamiltonian systems by eliminating the phase space variation restriction and providing an alternative, namely the use of unique Hamiltonian paths for each system-state, which also solves the accessibility problem and may hold potential applications in analyzing irreversible processes and systems with large phase space variations.

In the TMC-1 dark molecular cloud, a new chemical pathway involving small ethynyl cyclopentadiene isotopes, $C^{13}_{5}$-CCH-CPD and CCH-C$^{13}$-CPD, was detected for the first time. Using sensitive spectral data from the ALMA telescope, researchers determined the abundances of these rare isotopes as well as the previously observed CNCPD and CCH-CPD molecules. When combined with existing observations, a comprehensive analysis of ring-containing molecules in TMC-1 revealed that CCH and CN are the primary drivers for the addition of small atoms to polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons under cold interstellar conditions. The authors propose that low-energy photon processes, such as those occurring in dark molecular clouds, can facilitate the formation of such complex molecules by first creating excited barriers and then adding small atoms to the structure.

Attention mechanisms in Neural Machine Translation allow the model to
identify relevant source words when generating each target word. Traditional
attention models are limited because they only consider source words up until
that point. To address this issue, we propose an innovative Look-forward
Attention model that also takes into account target words yet to be generated.
By training a decoder-transformer on data truncated to match the vocabulary
of the current task, our model can look ahead when generating each target word.
Our experiments on the MWT and Google Machine Translation evaluation sets
demonstrate that our model outperforms the baseline NWATTN by significant
margins.

This paper presents a translational theory of technology, offering a framework for tracing the evolution of technical artifacts and practices. It examines the concept of translation, inspired by anthropological and sociological theories, and explores how technology evolves through the process of translating systems into related technologies. Furthermore, it considers how new ideas and technologies can emerge from a translation process and uses the development of grid computing as a case study to illustrate these concepts.

A newly devised framework, known as the Dissipative Combined Dark Fluid (DCDF), unifies several fundamental concepts, such as dark energy, dark matter, and fluid dynamics, into a singular theoretical framework. Rooted in General Relativity, the DCDF model leverages the field equations and conservation laws to investigate its implications, specifically in a flat, expanding universe. The model's dynamics are analyzed through both physical variables and redshift-based representations, resulting in an elaborate expression for its effective equation of state, which incorporates dissipative effects, and is further explored for its density evolution, and in terms of the Hubble parameter. The model's predictive capabilities are demonstrated through estimated values for the age of the universe, and its stability is assessed through the application of perturbation theory, ensuring its consistency and reliability.

In the field of education, curiosity is a vital skill that drives individuals to acquire new knowledge and engage in effective learning. However, due to its subjective nature, accurately measuring curiosity remains a significant hurdle in the creation of personalized learning systems. As a result, the development of system personalization tools that take curiosity into account has been significantly impeded. Our goal is to establish a robust framework for analyzing curiosity in group learning environments, utilizing a unique approach that combines self-reported data with automated analysis of written expressions, visual attention, and facial expressions显示的好奇心. Our in-depth examination of curiosity in this context involves several stages, including the collection of synchronized multimedia evidence, the creation of a publicly accessible dataset, and the application of text and visual attention processing techniques to explore the meaning of curiosity in this setting. Ultimately, our work paves the way for future research on understanding curiosity in educational environments and demonstrates the potential of a data-driven approach to analyzing complex phenomena.

We've developed a novel class of spatially correlated random effects, specifically Mat\'ern Gaussian processes adapted to graphs. Using a stochastic representation, these processes are linked to an underlying 'base' measure, which provides flexibility in specifying the graph's edge weights and the underlying space. A key characteristic of our approach is its ability to retain the marginal improvement of the covariance matrix, thereby facilitating efficient posterior computation through methods like nested sampling, stochastic gradient Markov chain Monte Carlo, and variational inference, which outperform traditional techniques like Gaussian process regression. We've demonstrated the benefits of our model through comparisons with alternatives, as well as in public health and environmental applications, where our approach has shown improved or comparable performance.

The effectiveness of map-based navigation systems and other navigational services relies on accurate digital representations of real-world environments. Although there are traditional methods for creating these representations, they are time-consuming and costly. The proposed approach takes advantage of a large number of mobile devices, such as buses and taxis, moving through city streets to identify and map road networks. By analyzing which areas with traffic receive the most data transmissions, the approach can efficiently use mobile devices' processing capabilities to map road networks at a system-wide level, balancing the amount of data collected with overall performance.

We investigated J/ψ decays into visible and invisible photon pairs to assess their ability to differentiate between various types of new physics represented by different types of higher-dimensional operators within neutrino and dark sector effective field theories. By analyzing LHC data, researchers found that J/ψ decay rates and asymmetries can provide meaningful constraints on the scales of new physics, with certain studies showing they can be comparable to or even exceed the constraints obtained from experiments involving neutral kaons and neutrino oscillations. Furthermore, focusing on J/ψ decays to a visible photon and any other undetectable particle, researchers discovered that a significant advantage exists over traditional searches for J/ψ decays into visible photon pairs, allowing for more stringent constraints on the scale of new physics relative to experiments involving neutral mesons and neutrino experiments.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the standard differential equation format, but this has not yet been published for equations that involve a $y'$ term. This missing implementation has now been completed and the new methods have been tested against problem scenarios, comparing both constant and variable stepsize approaches. Additionally, the development of appropriate stepsize control strategies has been adapted for variable stepsize SDIMSIMs.

This research generalizes multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis for analyzing complex, time-varying data sets that depend on multiple parameters. We are among the first to adapt this technique for data sets whose characteristics evolve over different dimensional time scales. An underlying geometry is crucial to adapting the method, which we illustrate with simple cases of linear and curved surfaces. A key component of the method is a new, flexible way to extract meaningful features from the data, extending traditional kernel techniques. We propose modifying the data's structure to reveal its spectrum and explore the effects of this change on the method's underlying mathematics. Numerical experiments demonstrate the method's ability to recover significant patterns and features from generated data sets. We also apply the method to analyze brain activity data obtained through scanning techniques, successfully identifying existing patterns and significant frequencies.

In the last few years, Automated Emotion Simulation (AES) has been heavily promoted as a highly reliable and emotionally authentic virtual interaction technology. Unfortunately, the current state of the art AES models are suffering from two significant issues - model dependability and model responsiveness are both severely compromised. This paper seeks to address the fundamental causes of these problems by identifying the pervasive use of security-stable methods, namely regularization and dropout, to mitigate overfitting in these models. Our rigorous experiments reveal that these methods inadvertently amplify model dependence and impede model responsiveness. Due to the unintended amplification of model dependence, the current AES models are both overly sensitive to minor variations in input data and excessively sensitive to model compression, resulting in models that are both insecure and inefficient. To better address these issues, this paper proposes a novel concept of security robustness, and two innovative security-aware optimizations - AES Secure SqueezeNet (ASS) and AES Secure Pruning Network (ASPN) by replacing the usage of regularization and dropout with representation learning. Our comprehensive evaluations across multiple datasets and tasks demonstrate that ASS and ASPN significantly reduce both model dependence and model responsiveness, and also outperform competing security robust techniques in emotion recognition performance.

In a one-dimensional simple random walk, the points where the path returns to the starting position divide the journey into isolated segments. This research explores the properties of these isolated segments, specifically their lengths. The study focuses on identifying conditions under which there is at least one segment meeting a specified size threshold. The research provides theoretical evidence that the probability of observing a significant segment remains constant as the number of possible review moments increases, and that this phenomenon holds true over the course of an infinitely long random walk. The study also derives the precise constant of probability from given initial conditions and simulation results for related quantities.

This study validates the plasma formation theory, specifically the transition from electron density plateau to $R^{-1/2}$ scaling, and experiments and plasma measurements for the IIsTAR helicon plasma generator.  A 1.1 m radius, 1.05 m depth 1.5T toroidal plasma chamber was used, and electron density was measured using plasma probes and plasma oscillations at various powers and magnetron modes.  At low power (50-100Scm$^{-3}$ electron density), increasing the plasma radius was achievable by increasing input power.  However, at higher density, the plasma density plateau could not be exceeded due to magnetron mode switching and plasma instability.  Increasing the number of magnetron rotations did not increase the electron density but rather resulted in plasma transition back to the plateau by reducing the effective radius by increasing plasma depth.  Intensity fluctuations in plasma spectroscopy did not support plasma instability but were found to be caused by plasma probes failing to capture volume-averaged density due to edge turbulence likely originating from ion transit oscillations.  Radio frequency (RF) reflection in the coaxial feed line was utilized to detect the plasma instability by region of interest (ROI) and found to be lower at the critical density plateau than at low power and high power regimes which exhibited lower impedance matching likely originating from ion transit oscillations.  Increasing the electron density beyond the plateau was achievable by reducing the effective plasma radius and was supported by theory

To control microbial populations, various strategies exist, including natural predators, substances that microbial genes naturally encode, and external methods like genetic engineering. 
This study delves into a biopesticide model based on microbes that consume plants and microbes that are nontoxic to the host. A mathematical representation of the model is examined for its feasible solutions and stability, as well as possible periodic patterns. 
Analysis of the model reveals the impact of microbial suppression on its dynamics, and numerical simulations are used to validate the analytical findings.

MWU-Net is a novel architecture for detecting nuclear units in medical images,
addressing its development challenges including an imbalanced dataset, varying
nuclei appearances, and close-proximity nuclei that create segmentation difficulties.
To mitigate these issues, we established a specialized dataset with balanced classes
and controlled complexity by filtering out difficult cases. Furthermore, to enhance
performance, a two-stage approach was implemented: initially, a classification stage
utilizes a pruned ResNet to identify nuclei units and assign balance class labels;
subsequently, an attention-based classification stage guides a fully convoluted network
to perform precise segmentation, focusing on the less under-represented class;
experimentation on our customized dataset demonstrates that MWU-Net outperforms base
networks in terms of accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score.

We establish a novel approach to prove that certain irreducible representations of a specific type of matrix group, special orthogonal or a symplectic group, over a larger field are uniquely identified by their local components within another field. This approach is innovative as it utilizes a method previously unapplied to this purpose, specifically involving 'compactly supported functions' and has been proven effective despite limitations of the underlying mathematical framework. Our strategy has successful applications in two scenarios where the larger field's underlying numbers are even and these elements are not equal to five and we demonstrate the desired uniqueness of the representation.

This research paper defines two novel graph properties: a graph G is considered to have an iterated line graph hamiltonian path (IHPP) if its (n-1)th iteration has a hamiltonian path, and a graph G is considered to have an iterated line graph hamiltonian cycle (IHHPC) if its (n-1)th iteration has a hamiltonian cycle, where n represents the number of iterations required for a line graph to become connected. Available results providing sufficient conditions for graphs to satisfy the properties of having an IHPP or IHHPC are discussed within this paper's framework.

Epidemiological indicators indicate a decreased infection rate in Italy beginning in early April 2020, an observation that we sought to explain by developing a non-intervention and an anti-inflammatory intervention mathematical model. These models were designed to simulate individual infection and death rates, with data drawn from the University of Padua and utilized across multiple scenarios, including those involving anti-inflammatory drug treatment. Our analysis and graphical results display the influence of specific parameters on infection and death rates, with the R0 value playing a significant role. We identified the unique solitary cell equilibrium points for both non-intervention and intervention scenarios, and calculated critical thresholds for cell stability. Furthermore, we explored how cell equilibrium stability can be influenced by the rate of cell priming, the rate of cell inhibition, and the rate of pyroptosis.
