While exploring strategies to accelerate convergence and improve transferability, we introduce the concepts of identifying and removing such outside factors. Building on this, we propose a series of approaches to eliminate these unrelated parameters and rewards by incorporating they can be independent of the agent's actions. Building on this, we introduce the concepts of identifying and eliminating such outside factors by introducing they can be independent of the agent's actions. While exploring strategies to accelerate convergence and improve transferability, we introduce the concepts of identifying and removing such outside factors by introducing they can be independent of the agent's actions.

The blockchain-based platform known as Tezos utilizes smart contracts to combine code and data in a way that allows for decentralized operation. As the Tezos ecosystem expands, based on computer language Refinement-type provides a way to verify the correct functioning of smart contracts through their complex interactions. This paper presents a validator called Helmholtz, capable of confirming the correctness of smart contracts by refining the capabilities of the underlying computer language. Helmholtz can also serve as a building block for contract generators capable of maintaining functionality across the life cycle of contracts like those used in the Tezos-based project KNOMOS.

Neural networks have been applied to various graph-structured data sets, lacking the sequential patterns found in images or text. A novel approach for designing graph-based neural networks is missing. This paper introduces a straightforward and adaptable method for developing neural networks on any type of data, including sequences, images, and social networks. A key aspect of this method is that it interprets a neural network's operation as a matching and filtering process. A Graph Convolutional Neural Network (GCNN) is derived using this approach and experimentally tested for improved performance over existing models in classification and segmentation tasks on dynamic graphs.

In a three-dimensional setting, we've identified a specific relativistic field theory that includes a scalar field with self-interaction, capable of forming "hairy" black hole solutions, in the limit of low speeds. This theory can be described by a Chern-Simons gauge action, making it possible to derive the properties of both "hairy" black holes and smooth, soliton-like solutions from this model. By applying a specific set of transformations to the Chern-Simons equations, we've demonstrated that these solutions correspond to those of pure gravity, confirming the relationship between "hairy" black holes and solitons. Moreover, we've found that a specific, stationary soliton solution can represent a black hole with a specific horizon, and we've explored how this correspondence holds for black holes with different properties.

A generalizable framework is introduced to expand upon previously found extensions of Chiral and Hermitian theories, incorporating membranes and chiral hermitian systems featuring k-point interactions. Specific examples are provided, including a k-dimensional analog to the q-ANM model, which can be modified to include chiral symmetry. Furthermore, a comprehensive set of conditions is established for 2k x 2k matrices to display non-trivial non-reversible symmetries. Lastly, a method to derive dynamical laws from these symmetric matrices is set forth, focusing on Hermitian membranes.

In traditional sonography and elastography imaging, reference lateral displacement estimation is typically done using a Virtual Origin (VO) approach, where the central element of the transducer array acts as a point source emitting ultrasound. Although VO methods are commonly used, they suffer from inaccurately large lateral displacements in the outer regions of the transmission beam. We introduce a virtual synthetic origin (VSO) method that better mimics the actual transducer element positions, providing more accurate displacement estimation. By applying a depth-dependent shift to VO data, we can recover the accuracy benefits of VSO without significantly increasing processing time relative to VO methods. Analysis using simulations, ex-vivo liver samples, and in-vivo liver samples demonstrates comparable improved results when comparing VO, VSO, and our modified VO approach using in-vivo data.

Algorithms described in papers are often difficult to follow due to complex mathematical formulas and acronyms. As demonstrations with robots become more common, there is a need to create clearer algorithms that are easier to both read and replicate. We have developed a template for presenting algorithms that eliminates obstacles to comprehension, including ambiguous notation, by using a step-by-step, pseudo-code-like code. We believe this approach can facilitate the easy replication of experiments and, if widely adopted, could set a new standard for publishing algorithmic procedures in academic settings. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by providing a clear, replicable method for generating image segmentation masks from depth maps.

We are interested in the Boolean algebra version of Ramsey theory for partially ordered sets, specifically those within the power sets of natural numbers. The concept of $\mathcal{B}n$-Ramsey property for a poset $P$ is defined by a positive integer $r$, where $\mathcal{B}k$-colorings of $2^n$ elements result in a sub-set with the same structure and color $P$. Some research has already been done on specific posets like strings and antichains. Our work extends this research to a new class of posets called $V$-shaped posets. The main findings of our work show that certain $V$-shaped posets do not have the $\mathcal{B}n$-Ramsey property for any $n$, and identify specific posets within this class that are not even locally $\mathcal{B}n$-Ramsey.

Recent advances in stream processing and machine learning library integration have made it feasible to apply and enhance advanced learning techniques on intricate, high-dimensional data sets. A fundamental yet critical challenge in this field is identifying the most effective way to represent an incoming data stream efficiently. In this paper, we tackle the dynamic $k$-means grouping problem for high-dimensional data, enabling non-deletion updates of existing data points and new parameters for added points. Formally modeling this problem, we develop a compact summary data structure that ensures a limited increase in computing time and memory usage during updates, and an algorithm generating a series of approximate optimal $k$-means groups from the updated summary. Additionally, we propose a straightforward summary construction and allocation algorithm, leveraging existing stream processing and machine learning library integration. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed method's superiority over existing dynamic $k$-means schemes on intricate, high-dimensional data sets.

The hypothetical pursuit and evasion competitions, often studied in mathematics, can be applied to model and solve real-world problems in various fields. We examine different hierarchical forms of pursuit-evasion competitions, including multiple agents chasing one, one chasing multiple, and divided scenarios, such as groups pursuing groups, individuals pursuing multiple groups, and so on. We explore the evaluation metrics for these hierarchical scenarios and discuss the evaluation methods for specific forms, such as one entity chasing two others and groups pursuing two entities.

Inspired by Freiling's nonintuitive result that circular real numbers are virtually nonexistent, a new concept, nontransitive circles, is introduced. Define an n-tuple of points on a unit circle as nontransitive if no single point is closer to more than half of the remaining points. It is now demonstrated that nontransitive real n-tuples are almost guaranteed, in contrast to nontransitive k-tuples, where k is a finite integer, which are entirely impossible. Additionally, this finds application in revealing the illusion of statistical independence, as previously shown in an earlier publication.

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained widespread acceptance and utilization in image reconstruction and denoising at low doses. A recent cycleGAN approach for low-dose computed tomography (CT) denoising showed promising results at moderate noise levels but struggled in less ideal conditions. We discovered that certain parts of the AdaIN CycleGAN architecture were redundant and formed the basis of our innovation. We developed a novel adaptive switchable AdaIN CycleGAN, which can seamlessly integrate both normal and inverted normalization modes within the generator. This updated architecture enables more effective fusion of images at low doses and is particularly effective in noisy, noisy environments. We verified the advantages of our proposed method through experiments on lung low-dose CT images and found that it significantly outperformed existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of visual quality and quantitative metrics.

Recent advancements in dialogue understanding using large-scale pre-trained models have been boosted by the contrast pre-training method. To harness the potential of the pre-trained models, we introduce a novel technique called SPACE-2: Semi-Supervised Pre-training with Tree-structured Comprehension Entities. This method utilizes both labeled and unlabeled dialogue data for contrast learning, based on the assumption that similar dialogues yield similar answers. To address the challenge of unlabeled data, we designed an effective technique to generate hard examples for comparison. Our experimentally determined optimal method involves grouping dialogues into the same comparison pair if they provide different answers to the same question. We applied SPACE-2 to three different dialogue understanding tasks and obtained significant performance gains over the baseline and other Pre-trained models on the MultiWC dialogues after the fine-tuning stage. According to the results, the model achieved a F1 score of 0.65 on the date extraction task, 0.43 on the MultiWC dialogues, and a Per-Document Accuracy of 0.29 in the dialogue summary task.

We establish the instantaneous geometric configuration of an ideal fluid universe that is conformal to a Ricci-Yamabe manifold and is driven by a scalar field that changes over time. Additionally, we prove that the ratio of the Yamabe constant to the scalar field is not equal to three times the cosmological constant. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the scalar field is constant when the energy density is greater than the cosmological constant and provides the eigenpotential of the soliton as the product of the Yamabe constant and the scalar field. We also prove that the soliton is expanding when the cosmological constant is greater than the energy density and is contracting when the cosmological constant is less than the scalar pressure. We demonstrate that the soliton is rigid when the torsion of the manifold is absent and is rotating when the soliton is rigid.

Research on the spin properties of distorted halo nuclei is advance by theoretical work which aims to describe how these nuclei behave as spinning entities. Our framework builds upon previous concepts, such as the collective spinning liquid drop, and incorporates the interaction between the shape and spin degrees of freedom through a generalized potential in a Hamiltonian approach. This allows us to examine a range of spinning two-component Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov mass operators, covering interacting particle-hole and particle-particle forces. By applying this approach to eccentric rotators, we investigate specific nuclei like $^{11}\mathrm{Li}$ and $^{6}He$, focusing on their ground states and excited states, as well as their response to external magnetic fields. Comparing our results to those from the time-dependent variational principle and relevant experiments, we discover distinct shape uncoupling effects, resulting in characteristic anomalies such as effective $g$-factor enhancements, resonant geometry, and resonance anti-Aharonov-Bohm shifts.

A common architecture in video super-resolution systems is the BSR3Flow, which effectively utilizes multi-frame information to restore complex regions in video content. Nevertheless, there are limited studies improving this network structure to cope with challenging scenarios like large motion and blur. To do this, we present a comprehensive evaluation of the 3-fold propagation and bilateral alignment mechanisms within the BSR3Flow architecture, highlighting their limitations, and proposing an upgraded configuration for each. Furthermore, we integrate these improvements into the BSR3Flow to create a novel network called video super-resolution with bilateral alignment and 3-fold propagation (VSR++). VSR++ utilizes the excellent temporal information utilization and frame-wise quality of BSR3Flow, yet significantly outperforms it in dealing with motion and blur. In our enhanced configuration, we incorporate a densely connected unified propagation (DUP) branch to facilitate information sharing among propagation branches and a refined bilateral alignment branch (RAB), which jointly optimize the propagation branches' features, to avoid conflicts during feature fusion. To demonstrate the superior performance of VSR++, we extensively evaluate it via numerous numerical results, visually comparing it with the original BSR3Flow and other advanced video super-resolution methods on diverse datasets, including Sinew w/blur, super-resolution video rendering (SRVR), and classic video super-resolution (CVSR) benchmarks, and visually comparing it with state-of-the-art methods on these benchmarks.

The potential for vector boson scattering (VBS) processes to become observable at the $\mu\mu$ collider, with an energy set at 10 TeV, is the focus of this study. The conditions necessary to ensure the clarity of these processes are examined, noting the advantage offered by the capability to rotate the detector and rotate the beam, which can be utilized to enhance the purity of the selected events. The optimal strategies for detecting the final states resulting from WW and ZZ processes in the lepton-plus-jet and four-lepton channels are demonstrated. Furthermore, certain constraints on the VBS signal are derived and validated using simulated data. Ultimately, the feasibility of an discovery of new physics beyond the Standard Model is assessed, revealing the potential for achieving a significant outcome in both channels, characterized by a sensitivity of approximately 5 sigma in both the WVBS and ZZVBS cases.

The paper argues that a modular model is crucial for applying the multi-task learning framework to reinforcement learning. Without a modular learning model, group thinking emerges in model-based multi-task reinforcement learning. As a result, the learned dynamics are robust but suboptimal, leading to destructive interference. Experiments showcase the negative effects of destructive interference and highlight how a modular approach can prevent it. Furthermore, the paper suggests using a modular neural network and a connectivity learning mechanism to establish task-specific connection patterns, thereby avoiding suboptimal robustness. Proposed methods are validated through comprehensive experimental evaluations.

This paper provides discrete and continuous approximations for the solution of a given equation $u_{t} = \Delta_{p}u^{q-1}$, where the right-hand side includes the $p$-Laplacian operator and the solution is subject to specific initial and boundary conditions. Our work extends previous research by considering a broader setting of complete, non-compact metric measure spaces with compact boundary. Additionally, the problem can be extended to a more general form of equations operated by $\partial_t u - \Delta_{p}u + W|\nabla u| = 0$ under Dirichlet conditions.

We delve into the foundational issues of mathematics, focusing on Godel's 1931 Incompleteness Theorems, which are known to be dependent on certain technical aspects. Notably, it is later revealed that the reliance on the non-axiomatic nature of mathematics allows for the derivation of both true, unprovable statements within a given system, as well as unprovable statements originating from genuine mathematical truths. This insight is achieved long before Godel's seminal work, simplifying the understanding of inherent limitations within formal systems.

In Clifford analysis, whole plane eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator D are categorized by their degree, and this classification is essential for developing a corresponding Dirac-Mehler-Fock transform. Unlike scalar functions, where differentiation reduces function degree by one, the Dirac operator divides functions of differentiability order k into eigenfunctions of various degrees from -1 to k+1, based on the application of the Dirac operator. This classification process involves using an algorithm based on D and the complex conjugation operator to decompose a function into its eigenfunction components, and it has been demonstrated that this process can result in an explicit formula for the transformation coefficients, particularly for analytic polynomials, which can be classified as the "three spheres theorem for eigenfunctions of Dirac operator", and this result plays a crucial role in developing the Dirac-Mehler-Fock transform.

This paper introduces a novel balanced balancing method to improve the efficiency of geospatial sampling in a sequence of locations. By incorporating a balanced approach to balancing, we can create a more balanced sequence of balances from multiple balanced lists of points, located in different areas. Using the concept of a balanced sequence, we can choose an optimal point from the multiple balanced lists, ensuring optimal performance through time. Adapting the calibration of a camera that is mounted on a robot's arm is essential for maintaining precise image capture, especially over extended periods or when the robot operates in unstructured environments. While there are various approaches to recalibrating a camera, many require an elaborate setup with known reference objects and multiple images from different angles. In this research, a novel method is proposed that relies on the guidance of a human from a single image to reconfigure a camera's six degrees of movement. The proposed approach first acquires a set of images based on controlled motions of the robot's arm, and then uses these images to adjust the calibration based on the guidance provided from a single image and corresponding labeled features. The results show high accuracy in recovering the camera's calibration, as evidenced by low errors in the computed parameters.

In solving inverse problems, researchers often encounter difficulties due to the solutions space being too vast and complex, a issue that can be alleviated by utilizing generative adversarial networks (GANs) to generate a simpler, lower-dimensional space. Through training, a generator function can create an optimized solutions space that accurately reflects the underlying data, thus facilitating the identification of the target posterior distribution during sampling. However, ensuring that the generated samples maintain a one-to-one correspondence with observed data during GAN training remains a significant challenge due to the collapse phenomenon associated with gradient-based optimization. To mitigate this issue, we propose introducing a regularization term into the discriminator objective function that penalizes excessive variance in the discriminator's output, a modification that encourages more robust sample generation and facilitates the extraction of an optimal posterior distribution in inference applications.

We examine linear fractional dynamics of the form x^(α) = Ax, where α is not equal to 1, and A represents a constant matrix. Our goal is to identify the conditions under which an invariant manifold exists in this system, and specifically we determine that an invariant manifold can be represented as y = S(y0), where S is an infinite series composed of non-fractional powers. It has been proven that S cannot equal 1, and thus there are no invariant planes in this system when the value of α is greater than 0 and less than 1, and where the diagonal elements of matrix A are not negative rational numbers with denominators equal to α. Consequently, there are no invariant planes in this system.

Next-generation wireless networks will utilize terahertz frequencies to overcome worsening mobile data rates per capita and high spectral demand by intensity-changing applications like holographic communication and neural link transfers. Nevertheless, signal degradation over long wavelengths hinders stable thz link establishment across multi-hop locations. This paper proposes a novel hierarchical beam training method for multi-hop terahertz links that first determines the feasible link hops and then independently refines the optimal beams at each hop. A reinforcement learning technique is applied to reduce the beam training overhead and acceleration techniques are explored to speed up the training process. Simulation results show that in comparison to conventional methods, the proposed technique cutting down beam training by roughly 25% while maintaining comparable overall performance.

Located in the Crab Nebula, pulsar B1133+16 has a high luminosity and is being observed to understand its interstellar environment. By analyzing scintillation patterns in its radio signals, researchers found that the interstellar medium in the northern part of the nebula has significantly higher irregularities than a nearby region outside the nebula. These results indicate the presence of more intense turbulent fluctuations in the interstellar medium within the northern part of the nebula.

This paper presents a novel generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limitations of WaveNet in generating audio signals, addressing its inefficiency due to the vast number of learnable filters and its inability to maintain quasi-periodicity in speech sounds. By analyzing signal quasi-periodicity from the梅尔倒谱系数 (Mel-Cepstral Coefficients, MCCs) and Mel-Cepstral Residuals (MCRs), this study proposes replacing the dilated convolution layer in Wavenet with two sets of pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural networks, utilizing previous frame outputs and corresponding latent codes to improve output performance. Experimental results indicate that Quasi-Periodic WaveNet outperforms Wavenet in both synthetic speech and music sounds, demonstrating substantial improvements in objective and subjective evaluations over generative adversarial network-based methods at similar network sizes.

This research presents a specialized annotation tool called MADARi, designed for comprehensive markup of Classical and Modern Arabic texts.  The annotation tool considers the written text in addition to the underlying spoken language during the markup process, requiring identification of all spoken language units and corresponding text segments in addition to character-level markup.  A key feature of MADARi is its incorporation of a automatic annotation system that speeds up the annotation process and enhances consistency, by suggesting text-segments identification and character-level markup.  The annotation tool can be accessed online via a public website, available at http://adar.ics.aizu.jp/MADARi/.

This report walks through the primary photochemical processes that can happen on temperate and highly inflated hot Jupiters, fueled by intense ultraviolet radiation from their host stars. The process by which molecular bonds are broken under UV light, as well as subsequent recombination events that can form new compounds are examined in detail. The document delves into the analysis of spectral changes using basic radiative transfer equations, taking into consideration the variations caused by molecular bonds being stretched, bent, or split, as well as the shifts in spectral lines due to the Doppler effects induced by the rapid rotation of these planets. The discussion is particularly relevant to the accurate interpretation of future high-resolution spectral data that will be obtained by next-generation telescopes such as EXTREME on the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) and HIRES on the Thirty Meter Telescope (TMT).

Our research suggests utilizing a model where the superconductor is connected to resistive leads, whose resistance decreases as power-law, to differentiate between a Majorana peak and other peaks in tunneling spectra. A model incorporating non-equilibrium physics and non-quasiparticle准粒子 distributions was established, and the tunneling current and spectra were simulated, resulting in a broadened zero-bias peak whose width can be managed by adjusting the resistance of the electrodes. Notably, the peak remains robust against variations in the ratio of the superconducting gap and the damping rate, and its shape is largely unaffected by the material's normal state Fermi energy.

The development of advanced computer vision systems has gained significant traction in the detection of road issues, including various techniques based on deep learning architectures convolved with image enhancement methods to address the challenge of reliably identifying defects under different lighting conditions. Despite these approaches, research efforts have mostly focused on laboratory settings, underserved areas, and controlled testing scenarios, lacking a comprehensive setup that encompasses all stages of the detection process from data collection to results presentation. This includes the need for specialized equipment, skilled operators, and software systems to manage data and generate comprehensive reports for further action plans, all while ensuring adherence to industry safety standards. To address these challenges, we have developed an innovative road defect detection system that leverages colorful road surfaces and deep learning technologies, enabling the accurate identification of potholes, signage, and other essential elements, even in low-light settings. This system has been put to test in multiple real-world scenarios on colorful roads and successfully detected over 1000 potholes in a single run, even without the need for data cleaning stages, all while ensuring industry safety standards are met, as verified by a professional inspection company. To showcase the comprehensive nature of our road inspection process, we have created an innovative smart platform called RoadAtlas that integrates the entire defect detection workflow from data collection to final presentation, including a results dashboard and the ability to export comprehensive reports in PDF format, ready for further action plans.

Recent years have seen a significant adaptation of Graph Neural Networks to various types of data, with a notable limitation being their ineffacy with temporal graphs that exhibit orientation-dependent causality. This causal asymmetry is prevalent in numerous temporal graphs, often aligning with the directional properties of real-world data. Traditional RNN-GNN architectures are well-suited for processing such time-stamped data but struggle with spatial graph patterns. Our proposed Lorentzian Graph Neural Network addresses this challenge by utilizing a Lorentzian graph as an underlying architecture. This novel approach leverages the natural directional properties of time-scale graphs and for es a RNN component. Our evaluation results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that L-GNN outperforms traditional RNN-GNN, proving its efficacy in handling time-dependent data.

The classical structural acoustic interaction can be viewed as the limit of progressive mechanical engagements, and this research examines the microscopic characteristics of this structure in detail.  A key finding reveals that slight engagements result in structural acoustic behavior, but we also investigate a broader scenario where the engagement factor includes the small parameter. This limit represents a modified structural acoustic interaction, and the research establishes its fundamental properties, addressing questions related to coercivity, compactness, and convergence. These theoretical foundations enable approximation methods for optimization problems involving optimized geometric engagements.

In complex networks, separating useful information from noise can be a challenging task, particularly when signals are mixed with random noise. We demonstrate a method to accomplish this when the network consists of optomechanical resonators and the noise is thermal in nature. Our method involves creating a specific steady-state where a specific mode in one resonator can be replicated precisely in a corresponding mode in another resonator, even when the two are not directly connected. Achieving this coherence transfer can be done by adjusting the system's damping rates and applying a specific control to minimize the impact of noise. Notably, this method works for both types of optomechanical interactions and can potentially be applied to applications such as quantum communication and computation.

We examine an expansion of modal $\mu$-calculus that accommodates a variety of formulas and determines its basic properties. Its structure enables classic modal $\mu$-calculus to be viewed as a subset, along with the capability to jointly transcendite and infinitary connectives. Furthermore, we establish a bisimulation equivalence for this enhanced calculus and demonstrate its capability to transitively and infinitary connectives for the modal $\mu$-calculus.

Research on how people make decisions is heavily influenced by efficient process theories which seek to rationally explain behavior. One significant finding from this research is that people tend to devalue future rewards more than anticipated. This study introduces a new delay discounting framework, efficient exponential DDM, that combines this irrationally Devaluing future with the assumption of rational decision-making. Key results from this framework include predictions on how people's preferences for immediate and future rewards, their willingness to take risks, and their discount rates are interconnected in complex ways. A crucial concept from this study is the efficient devaluation point, which represents the moment when people's discount rates for time are directly related to their devaluation of future time. This relationship enables predictions on how people's discounting behavior changes over time and provides the basis for deriving testable hypotheses in this area.

We've identified a Harmonic Gauge in Substantial General Relativity that aligns with the 4 constraints out of 10 in the harmonic coordinate system. The full harmonic coordinate system can be achieved using the new gauge conditions proposed in this research. The new conditions proposed in this research allow for linearizing the gravitational potential's wave equation. The new gauge conditions proposed in this condition share similarities with the semi-tensorial character of the Christoffel symbols. The new gauge conditions can be changed into a covariant form, the Harmonic-like Gauge, which corresponds to weak gravitational fields, and can be related to other theories, such as Weyl's Unified Field Theory and Einstein-Cartan Theory.

A signed graph $\sigma\mathbf{X}$ is considered a limit if there's a sequence of its finite counterparts $\sigma X_n$ whose sizes tend to infinity, while maintaining the same homomorphism ratios to another signed graph $\mathbf{Y}$. It has been established that any oriented graph requires at least three orientations. Conversely, we prove that any EDC of a oriented graph $\mathbf{X}$, denoted as $\mathbf{X'}$, satisfies the condition that $\chi(\mathbf{X'})\leq\chi(\mathbf{X})$. This implication suggests that if an EDC exists for $\mathbf{X}$, then $\chi(\mathbf{X})\geq 3$. For a quantum system in thermal equilibrium, we've developed a method to visually represent its thermal state using Weyl-Wigner space, allowing us to see how its behavior converges with classical systems as the Planck constant approaches zero. This approach enables the application of thermal equilibrium conditions, such as those from the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, in a way that is consistent with the system's thermal state. By utilizing a single, unified framework, we can systematically analyze the thermal equilibrium of Heisenberg-Weyl systems through a transformation of a linear vector space, ensuring that any represented thermal equilibrium state complies with fundamental physical laws. Furthermore, our method can be employed to analyze and design quantum systems that operate optimally within a thermal equilibrium environment.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been subject to extensive discussion, often accompanied by substantial confusion. Within a simplified, two-level system, we aim to demonstrate, through basic principles, that such temperatures are indeed real and provide a refined version of the two-spin system's Hamiltonian, as first described by R. Kubo, to achieve this goal.

The classification of histological images in pathology assists medical professionals in diagnosing and treating patients. However, manually analyzing these images requires extensive expertise and time, resulting in varied quality productions. Automatic diagnosis systems can efficiently diagnose and treat patients but often struggle with accuracy. Even when they perform well, system predictions still require pathological verification. Advanced technologies, such as artificial intelligence, have enhanced diagnostic system performance and reduced workload for pathology professionals. However, these technologies often operate as complex black boxes, hindering the understanding of prediction mechanisms by pathology professionals. This research presents a comprehensive dataset of annotated colorectal polyp images, containing approximately 4000 examples that have been classified and evaluated for dysplasia by pathology professionals. This dataset, along with its detailed metadata, is intended to support the development of automated diagnosis systems, such as those that combine the efforts of multiple pathology experts to improve accuracy and transparency through the explanation of prediction mechanisms.

A new numerical method has been developed to solve time-harmonic acoustic scattering problems, where the objective is to determine the associated acoustic field. This method uses traditional approximation techniques and can efficiently handle complex scenarios, including those with irregular domains, irregular boundaries, and frequent wavelength-to-domain sizing. The method transforms the problem from its original time-harmonic form to a series of equivalent multi-dimensional exterior scattering problems, each corresponding to a different integer. As the frequency of the system increases, the corresponding integer becomes larger, thereby enabling the adaptation of suitable high-frequency numerical techniques. Notably, the method does not require the domain sizing to conform to specific multiple of the wavelength requirements, even at higher frequencies. Instead, the method gradually converges to the accurate solution as the mesh and/or the discretization of the spatial domain are refined.

We analyze specific isotopic ratios in Chelyabinsk and Benenitra meteorites, suggesting that the meteorites, which originate from the inner Solar System, are products of moist rock-metal astroidal binaries that collided. The presence of water within these meteorites, along with distinct D/H isotopic ratios, suggest that the parent asteroids were indeed wet. Statistical calculations indicate that the meteorites resulted from the collision of such binaries post-2013 for Chelyabinsk and around 2009 CE for Benenitra. Molecular simulations suggest that the detected D2 proportions would not be achievable in the presence of significant H2 gas, suggesting that the isotopic ratios in these meteorites suggest the parent asteroids were volatile-rich. The Benenitra and Chelyabinsk meteorites provide vital evidence for the presence of water within the early solar system, suggesting that their data may help inform planetary formation theories and aid in reevaluating the textural features found in other meteorites, including those found on Earth, such as the Allende CAIs.

Specifically, we establish an explicit connection between the complete-set-of-excitation-energy and the representations-of-the-affine-quantum-algebra, represented-by-highest-weight, singular, and mixed-state-representations. Our theory-is-verified-through-rigorous-numerical-density-matrix-eigenvalue-renormalization-group-extrapolations.

Voice translation traditionally relies on available language pairs, but our research
introduces the challenging task of translating speech without prior knowledge of
the involved languages. We call this task zero-shot voice translation and test it
against the more accessible scenario where speakers have some familiarity with
at least one of the languages, known as familiar-language translation. A key
innovation is a new dataset, BuWaLa, synthesized from real speech, containing 36
language pairs across eight different languages. We examine these languages'
writing systems and ortho-phonetic properties to understand their impact on the
task. Through analyses of BuWaLa, we explore the effects of metadata and
acoustic modeling on performance, using both marginally informative and fully
informative training data. We use metrics like entropy and cross-entropy to
assess the complexity of the data and evaluate the results using human listening
tests and automatic metrics. Our findings on BuWaLa offer insights into the
limits of current speech translation models and highlight the challenges posed
by writing systems and languages that are entirely unknown.

We examine the connection between an object's optical properties and a electromagnetic wave's multipolar characteristics, specifically how several physical features interact with distinct modal characteristics. This study presents an efficient computational framework for calculating scattering and optical features by first decomposing a particle's geometry and material properties into a sum of three-dimensional elements, then utilizing an extended FADOM approach to derive the scattering, optical projection, and multipolar decomposition results. This method efficiently converts complex three-dimensional problems into manageable two-dimensional plots, significantly reducing computational time. We demonstrate the efficiency of this approach by accurately calculating scattering patterns and resonance features that a two-dimensional multipolar approach would struggle to achieve.

This study introduces two new concepts: double Young-Capelli bitableaux and the Schur altered symmetric functions, the latter being a combination of the former. We demonstrate that the Schur altered symmetric functions relate to the characters of the general linear group. Additionally, our findings provide a connection between the Young-Capelli character formula and the revised framework.

Within the most minimal scoto-seesaw model, we investigate the consistency of the standard model vacuum, and we study the connections between neutrino and dark matter properties. The model's simplicity demands at least three right-handed neutrinos, which results in a minimum of three dark matter stability portals. We calculate the range of dark matter mass that is compatible with experimental data, and within this range, we determine the allowable neutrino mass. We also examine the implications of initial conditions on vacuum stability, and we analyze how these conditions impact dark matter mass in relation to a specific parameter. Furthermore, we discover that a particular set of initial conditions can be achieved when neutrino and dark matter masses are closely related, and we find that the majority of stable dark matter scenarios fall within a specific mass region.

We utilized real-time time-dependent density functional theory to analyze the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ orbital mixing in four 4d and 5d transition metal compounds, specifically Sr1-Ca1 LaMnO3, Sr0-La2 LuMnO3, Sr2-Nd2 MnO4(MnO3)2, and Pr2-Sr2 MnO6(O)2. Our calculations demonstrated that the system's ground state can incorporate all six d-orbital degrees of freedom when the site symmetry allows for the orbital mixing. Spin-orbit coupling has a significant impact on the system's electronic structure and can be utilized to distinguish between these systems and those where only the $t_{2g}$ orbitals are active. Moreover, the system's effective spin-orbit coupling can be related to the system's constituent parts. Our findings provide a fundamental understanding of orbital mixing within these systems, which can serve as building blocks for more complex scenarios involving orbital activity.

In this study, we extend the notion of Lagrangian algebra from toric varieties to a broader class of varieties, incorporating those that are birationally equivalent to toric varieties. For the algebras developed, we demonstrate preservation of key properties found in toric varieties, specifically the operation of deformation and localization techniques. Notably, our research enables the application of localization techniques to retrieve data from compactified spaces from their affine counterparts. This research may be viewed as a classical analog to certain concepts in categorified prelog structures.

Fake news and misinformation are widespread issues in society, particularly
misleading and deceptive medical information can have severe consequences.
Deep fakes and manipulation are sophisticated technologies used for generating
deceptive information; however, they are hard for ordinary people to detect.
This project aims to employ image manipulation techniques to create artificial
diseases from healthy X-rays. Several manipulation methods were tested, including
GAN, Auto-Encoder, and PCA, to see which produced the most natural-looking
images. Several radiologists assessed the results, and PCA was found to be the
most effective, creating natural images that were easily identifiable as containing
specific illnesses. This outcome is expected, given PCA's simplicity makes it
more prone to generating artificial data with clear patterns, whereas PCA's
ability to generate concise representations may make its PCA PC's invisible in
X-rays and thus harder to detect. This project's limitations include PCA's
ability to create only linear representations, and PCA's inability to generalize
to unseen data, making it necessary for patients to have an X-ray taken anew
if their data needs to be altered. This project's findings are for testing and
validation purposes only, and such deep fakes and manipulation should not be used
to generate artificial or deceptive medical information.

ViDaExpert is a visual inspection tool that enables effective examination and
understanding of complex data sets. It incorporates the latest research in
vector visualization, combining techniques for 2D/3D projection and object
interpretation in a user-friendly interface. The tool is language- and database-
agnostic, ensuring broad compatibility. It is particularly suited for examining
high-dimensional data and can be utilized in various fields such as machine
learning, text analysis, and bioinformatics.

This paper provides an algebraic calculation of Newtonian potential values on a two-dimensional flat surface, using simple rectangular and circular measurement domains. We derive specific formulas for these calculations within defined boundaries, as well as on the edges of those boundaries. Notably, our solutions are efficient and can be updated rapidly when only the position or movement of mobile targets changes, thanks to the use of basic polynomial transformations. The efficiency and adaptability of our approach have been verified through tests run on a computer, demonstrating its valuable utility for real-time applications, particularly when combined with algorithms used to track moving objects, known as Voronoi algorithms.
